article.headline: Citrini's Boring Bet: The Analog Stack Between the Grid and the GPU
article.lede: For two years, the loud trade in artificial-intelligence equities has been compute, optics and memory. A research shop on Substack argues the quietest corner of the supply chain — the capacitors, magnetics and power-conversion chips that sit between a wall socket and a Blackwell die — has finally begun to re-rate, and that most investors still are not paying attention.
article.body:
On the third of May, Citrini Research's account on X claimed that its 'AI Power Plumbing' basket — a portfolio of analog semiconductor and passive-component names — was the best-performing thematic basket in its universe since the recent equity-market lows, with a chart marking a 163.55 percent gain. The thesis, the post says, was first laid out in late 2024, when the firm flagged the 'analog stack between the grid and the GPU' as 'boring, deeply cyclical, and an asymmetric corner of the AI buildout the market kept ignoring.'

A brief glossary is in order, because the names on Citrini's list are mostly unfamiliar outside specialist desks. Analog semiconductors do not crunch ones and zeros; they translate between the messy physical world (voltage, current, heat, motion) and the digital logic that consumes them. Inside any AI server, the journey from a 13.8-kilovolt feeder line to the 0.65-volt rail that actually feeds an Nvidia GPU passes through several stages of conversion. Each stage requires power-management integrated circuits, discrete power transistors (so-called MOSFETs), inductors and magnetics to store and shape current, and capacitors — chiefly multi-layer ceramic capacitors, or MLCCs — to smooth voltage transients. A modern Nvidia GB300 rack is reported to contain roughly thirty thousand MLCCs and dedicates close to half the volume of its power shelves to capacitor-based energy storage, used to absorb the millisecond-scale current spikes that come when thousands of GPU cores wake at once. That is what Citrini calls 'plumbing.'

The 'dual China/Auto-cycle overhang' Citrini referenced has a concrete meaning. Through 2023 and 2024 the analog sector was punished twice over. First, automotive and industrial customers — historically the most reliable buyers of analog chips — worked off the inventory they had hoarded during the pandemic shortage, sending revenues sharply lower at companies such as STMicroelectronics, ON Semiconductor and Analog Devices. Second, a wave of Chinese domestic competitors, supported by Beijing's drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency, began pricing aggressively in commodity power devices, compressing margins for incumbents. Investors treated the entire group as a value trap: cheap, but tied to two cycles that refused to turn.

That appears to have changed. Texas Instruments — at roughly twenty percent share, the largest pure-play analog maker — reported first-quarter 2026 revenue of $4.83 billion, with the analog segment up 22 percent year-on-year and data-centre revenue up roughly 90 percent, according to coverage by 24/7 Wall St. and Manufacturing Dive. Murata Manufacturing, the Japanese MLCC giant, has reportedly moved to raise prices on AI-server and automotive-grade capacitors by 15 to 35 percent and projects fiscal-2030 AI-server MLCC demand at 3.3 times fiscal-2025 levels. Monolithic Power Systems, which displaced Vicor as the dominant supplier of high-density power modules to Nvidia's H100 generation, has guided its enterprise-data segment to 50-percent-plus growth and is positioning to capture roughly 70 percent of sockets on Nvidia's forthcoming Vera Rubin platform.

The interesting question, and the one Citrini's post implicitly raises, is which names have already re-rated and which have not. Texas Instruments and Monolithic Power are no longer cheap on any conventional measure. The smaller names on the list — Alpha and Omega Semiconductor, Vishay, Diodes Incorporated, Allegro MicroSystems — and the Japanese passives houses Murata, TDK, Nippon Chemicon and Sumida have moved less, in part because their exposure to AI is diluted by automotive and industrial revenue that is only beginning to recover. Wolfspeed, the silicon-carbide specialist, is a separate story altogether: it emerged from a Chapter 11 restructuring in late 2025 after Chinese substrate competition collapsed pricing on six-inch wafers from roughly $1,500 to $500.

A caveat on Citrini's headline number. Citrini Research, founded in 2023 by James van Geelen, a former independent analyst whose early calls on Silicon Valley Bank, GLP-1 obesity drugs and Nvidia gave the firm its reputation, sells most basket-level performance behind a paid Substack. The 163 percent figure shown in the chart cannot be independently verified from public sources, and 'since the recent market lows' is an unspecified start date that flatters any rebound. Whether the analog cycle has another leg or has already done most of its work is, as ever, a question the prices themselves will eventually answer.

concepts.definition: Citrini Research's coinage for the chain of unglamorous components that step electricity down from a data-centre's high-voltage feed to the sub-1-volt rail consumed by an AI accelerator: power-management ICs, discrete transistors, inductors, magnetics and bulk and ceramic capacitors. None of it computes, but none of it can be skipped.

Industry shorthand for the dollar value of components a given supplier sells into a single server. As AI racks have grown denser and more power-hungry, the analog and passive-component bill of materials per rack has risen sharply — the GB300 generation, for example, uses roughly thirty thousand MLCCs, several times a conventional server.

A small ceramic component that stores and releases tiny amounts of electrical energy on demand, smoothing voltage on a circuit board. AI servers consume them in the tens of thousands per unit because GPU power draws spike and collapse on millisecond timescales; high-capacitance, low-resistance grades dominate the high-end segment supplied chiefly by Murata, TDK, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Taiyo Yuden.

The block in a server or rack that converts incoming AC mains into the regulated DC voltages the rest of the system uses. In an AI rack a PSU is largely full of bulk capacitors and discrete power semiconductors; Nvidia's GB300 design dedicates roughly half the internal volume of its power shelves to capacitor-based energy storage.

The combination of two headwinds that depressed analog-semiconductor stocks through 2023-2024: a deep inventory correction in their largest end markets, automotive and industrial, and aggressive price competition from Chinese domestic suppliers benefiting from state-supported capacity expansion.

article.fact_check: The 163.55% return figure shown on the basket chart is sourced from Citrini Research's internal performance attribution and is not independently verifiable from public filings. The phrase 'since the recent market lows' does not specify a start date. Citrini's claim that the firm flagged the analog/AI-power thesis at the end of 2024 cannot be confirmed without a paid Substack subscription, but is consistent with the firm's published cadence of 'State of the Themes' notes and with their public Q4 2024 review. Texas Instruments Q1 2026 results, Murata's price-increase reporting, the GB300 MLCC and capacitor figures, and Wolfspeed's late-2025 restructuring are well-documented in the trade press.

ticker_txn.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
ticker_txn.blurb: The largest pure-play analog-semiconductor maker in the world by revenue, with roughly twenty percent share of the analog market. Texas Instruments designs and manufactures power-management chips, signal-chain devices and embedded processors used in industrial machinery, automobiles and, increasingly, AI servers. Its strategy is unusual in the industry: it owns and operates several 300-millimetre wafer fabs in the United States, giving it a long-term cost advantage against fab-light competitors, but also requiring a multi-year capital-spending programme that compressed free cash flow through 2023-2024.
ticker_txn.recent: Q1 2026 revenue came in at $4.83 billion, ahead of the $4.53 billion consensus, with analog-segment revenue up 22 percent year on year and data-centre revenue up roughly 90 percent. Capital expenditure dropped 40 percent year on year to $676 million as the 300mm fab build-out tapers, and free cash flow rose to $1.40 billion. The company has also announced selective price increases of 15 to 85 percent on certain analog products effective April 2026, in line with similar moves by Analog Devices, Infineon and Murata. The stock is up roughly 50 percent year-to-date through April 2026.

ticker_mchp.name: Microchip Technology Incorporated
ticker_mchp.blurb: Microchip Technology is a leading supplier of 8/16/32-bit microcontrollers and analog semiconductors, with a deep power-management portfolio covering PMICs, LDO regulators, DC-DC controllers, gate drivers for MOSFETs and IGBTs, and SiC gate drivers under its mSiC brand. It is one of the largest suppliers of mixed-signal and connectivity ICs for industrial, automotive, aerospace, and data-centre applications. Its Digitally Enhanced Power Analog (DEPA) controllers and 600V gate driver families address the high-voltage side of AI server power delivery, while its broad PMIC lineup targets point-of-load regulation for FPGAs, MPUs, and ASICs in compute racks.
ticker_mchp.recent: Microchip reported Q3 FY2026 (quarter ending December 2025) net sales of $1.186 billion, up 15.6% year-over-year and beating guidance, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.44 against a $0.39 consensus. CEO Steve Sanghi cited broad-based recovery across end markets, non-GAAP gross margins expanding from 52% to 60.5%, and strong bookings building into the March 2026 quarter. Q4 FY2026 guidance was set at $1.26 billion (midpoint), representing roughly 30% year-over-year growth, with EPS of $0.48–$0.52. The company also introduced a new 600V gate driver family and the MCP16701 PMIC targeting AI, high-performance computing, and data-centre applications in early 2026.

ticker_stm.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
ticker_stm.blurb: STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor group covering microcontrollers, sensors (MEMS), and — most relevant to the AI power-plumbing thesis — a broad power-semiconductor portfolio spanning SiC MOSFETs (STPOWER Gen 4), GaN devices, silicon IGBTs, and power-management ICs. ST is one of only a handful of vendors with an end-to-end 800 VDC power-conversion solution for AI data centres, offering complete reference designs from 800V bus-to-50V, 12V, and 6V conversion using its own SiC and GaN silicon. The company serves automotive, industrial, and, increasingly, hyperscale data-centre customers.
ticker_stm.recent: ST reported Q1 2026 revenue of $3.10 billion, up 23% year-over-year and above consensus of $3.04 billion, with Q2 2026 guidance of ~$3.45 billion. In March 2026 the company announced expanded 800 VDC power-conversion products (12V and 6V architectures) developed to the NVIDIA 800 VDC reference design and showcased at NVIDIA GTC 2026. In February 2026 ST disclosed a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar engagement with Amazon Web Services to supply semiconductors for AWS compute and AI data-centre infrastructure. Management projects data-centre revenue exceeding $500 million in 2026 and surpassing $1 billion in 2027.

ticker_on.name: onsemi (ON Semiconductor Corporation)
ticker_on.blurb: onsemi designs and manufactures intelligent power and sensing semiconductors, with a particular focus on silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs and modules under the EliteSiC brand, IGBT power modules, intelligent power modules (IPMs), and gate drivers. The company is a dominant SiC supplier to EV traction inverters and has been rapidly expanding into AI data-centre power delivery, supplying high-efficiency SiC and MOSFET solutions for GPU server power stages. Onsemi claims to be the first vendor to scale vertical GaN production, with 700V and 1,200V devices addressing AI server PSU and rack-level power conversion.
ticker_on.recent: Onsemi reported Q1 2026 revenue of $1.513 billion, above the guidance midpoint, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.64 versus the $0.61 consensus. CEO Hassane El-Khoury stated AI data-centre revenue grew more than 30% sequentially and more than doubled year-over-year in Q1 2026, well ahead of the company's earlier guidance for high-teens growth. Q2 2026 revenue guidance was set at $1.535–$1.635 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $0.65–$0.77. Management reiterated an expectation that AI data-centre revenue will double year-over-year across all of 2026, supported by broader chip-vendor adoption of EliteSiC and new 900V SiC design wins with EV/ESS customers including Geely, NIO, and Sineng Electric.

ticker_aosl.name: Alpha and Omega Semiconductor Limited
ticker_aosl.blurb: A mid-cap supplier of discrete power devices, wide-bandgap (silicon-carbide and gallium-nitride) transistors, power-management integrated circuits and modules. AOSL is the kind of name Citrini groups under 'AI power plumbing': it does not appear on any AI-headline list, but its MOSFETs and gate drivers sit inside intermediate-bus converters and point-of-load stages on AI server boards, where current densities now exceed 400 amps per device. The company operates a hybrid manufacturing model, with internal fabs in Oregon and joint-venture capacity in China.
ticker_aosl.recent: In October 2025 AOSL announced a portfolio of silicon-carbide and gallium-nitride parts aimed at Nvidia's 800-volt-DC rack architecture, the next generation of power distribution for megawatt-scale AI factories. In March 2026 it introduced 25-volt and 80-volt MOSFETs in advanced packaging targeting AI-server intermediate-bus and point-of-load applications, with continuous current ratings up to 405 amps. The stock has been volatile but is among the smaller analog names that have not yet rerated as aggressively as TXN or MPWR, leaving more headline AI optionality.

ticker_vsh.name: Vishay Intertechnology, Inc.
ticker_vsh.blurb: Vishay is one of the world's largest manufacturers of discrete semiconductors (MOSFETs, diodes, rectifiers) and passive electronic components (resistors, inductors, capacitors), making it a two-sided play on the AI server power-plumbing build-out. On the passive side, its vPolyTan polymer tantalum capacitors and IHLE inductors are design-in components for Nvidia Blackwell GB200 server power-supply units. On the semiconductor side, Vishay's PowerPAK MOSFETs, DrMOS integrated power stages, VRPower buck regulators, and SiC Schottky diodes populate the voltage-regulation and power-conversion circuitry of AI racks. The company is executing a multi-year capacity expansion centred on a new 12-inch wafer fab.
ticker_vsh.recent: Vishay reported Q4 2025 revenue of $800.9 million, up 1.3% sequentially, with full-year 2025 revenue of $3.07 billion. The Q4 book-to-bill ratio rose to 1.20 overall (1.27 for semiconductors, 1.13 for passives), and ending backlog reached 4.9 months — the strongest demand signal in several quarters. Management attributed growth partly to confirmed design wins in Nvidia GB200 AI servers across both MOSFET and vPolyTan capacitor lines. Q1 2026 guidance was $800–$830 million with 2026 CapEx of $400–$440 million, the majority directed to the 12-inch fab in what management called the peak of the five-year expansion. The CEO described the company as ready to accelerate on factory utilisation and margin recovery in 2026.

ticker_diod.name: Diodes Incorporated
ticker_diod.blurb: Diodes Incorporated is a fabless/hybrid analog and discrete semiconductor company serving automotive, industrial, computing, consumer, and communications markets. Its product portfolio for the AI power-plumbing story includes power MOSFETs, half-bridge and high/low-side gate drivers (600V), smart load switches for GPU and ASIC power domains, AC-DC controllers, DC-DC switching regulators, and LDO voltage references — all targeting server mainboards, power-delivery units, PCIe switches, and networking infrastructure. The company differentiates on a flexible hybrid manufacturing model and broad application-specific standard product (ASSP) coverage across low-to-medium voltage power rails.
ticker_diod.recent: Diodes reported Q4 2025 revenue of $391.6 million, up 15.4% year-over-year and ahead of the $387.7 million consensus, marking the highest annual revenue growth since 2021 at 13% for full-year 2025. CEO Gary Yu outlined a long-term target of $2.5 billion in revenue with $1 billion in gross profit. Q1 2026 guidance called for revenue of ~$395 million (±3%), representing approximately 19% year-over-year growth. Note: Q1 2026 results are scheduled for May 7, 2026, and were not yet reported at the time of writing; Q4 2025 is the most recent completed quarter available.

ticker_adi.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
ticker_adi.blurb: Analog Devices is one of the two largest analog semiconductor companies in the world (alongside Texas Instruments), with deep expertise in signal-chain ICs, data converters, and — critical for AI servers — power-management products including hot-swap controllers, multiphase voltage regulators, power-system management ICs (PSMICs), and DC-DC power stages. ADI's LTC4284/4286/4287 hot-swap family protects 48V AI rack infrastructure, while its MAX20790 and related multiphase controllers regulate power to GPUs and accelerators at the point-of-load. The company is also a leading supplier of 800 VDC first-stage conversion solutions designed to NVIDIA's high-voltage DC reference architecture for AI factories.
ticker_adi.recent: ADI reported Q1 FY2026 (quarter ending January 2026) EPS of $2.46 versus the $2.31 consensus, with revenue of $3.16 billion supported by a 50% year-over-year increase in data-centre revenue. AI and data-centre exposure now accounts for roughly one-fifth of total revenues. Q2 FY2026 guidance was set at $3.5 billion (±$100 million), with non-GAAP EPS of $2.88 (±$0.15) and adjusted operating margin of ~47.5%. In August 2025 ADI announced its first 800 VDC hot-swap and first-stage power solutions targeting NVIDIA intelligent platform management, with >98% conversion efficiency. The company has seen accelerating adoption of 48V/54V intermediate-bus converters and smart power stages for vertical power delivery in AI racks.

ticker_ifnny.name: Infineon Technologies AG
ticker_ifnny.blurb: Infineon Technologies is a global power-semiconductor leader headquartered in Munich, Germany, trading on US markets as an ADR (IFNNY). Its product lineup for AI server power delivery includes OptiMOS and CoolMOS MOSFETs, high-density quad-phase power modules (OptiMOS TDM2454xx, 280A in a 10x9mm footprint), XDP digital hot-swap and protection controllers for 48V AI racks, EiceDRIVER isolated gate drivers supporting SiC and GaN topologies, and high-voltage GaN reference designs for LLC converters running at 800V input. Infineon is a preferred power-silicon partner in NVIDIA's 800V HVDC reference architecture for next-generation AI data centres.
ticker_ifnny.recent: Infineon closed FY2025 (ending September 2025) with revenue of €14.66 billion and significantly raised its AI power revenue target to approximately €1.5 billion in FY2026, citing rapidly rising AI infrastructure demand. Revenue for the quarter ending December 2025 was $4.26 billion, up 16.8% year-over-year. In Q1 FY2026 the company announced new HV GaN reference designs for AI server power architectures and expanded its XDP digital protection family with the XDP711-001 48V hot-swap controller. A new Smart Power Fab in Dresden is on track to open in summer 2026. FY2026 guidance calls for moderate total revenue growth, with AI power as the primary growth driver against softer automotive and industrial demand, and adjusted gross margin in the low-forties percent range.

ticker_mpwr.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
ticker_mpwr.blurb: A fab-light analog company that designs high-density power-management integrated circuits — the chips that step a server's intermediate-bus voltage down to the sub-1-volt rail an AI accelerator actually consumes. MPWR moved from a broad-based analog supplier into the dominant provider of GPU-adjacent power modules during the H100 generation, displacing the incumbent Vicor at Nvidia. Its modules are characterised by very high current density and tight integration, which matter enormously as AI racks push past 100 kilowatts.
ticker_mpwr.recent: In early 2026, management raised the floor on its enterprise-data growth target to 50-percent-plus from a prior 30-to-40 percent range, citing acceleration in Nvidia Blackwell shipments. Analyst notes suggest MPWR may take roughly 70 percent of power-management sockets on the forthcoming Vera Rubin GPU platform (VR200 NVL144 and R200 HGX), potentially adding more than $100 million to 2026 estimates. The stock has gained roughly 90 percent over the trailing twelve months and trades near all-time highs, leaving the AI exposure largely in the price.

ticker_vicr.blurb: Vicor Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, and markets modular power components and power systems for converting electrical power in electrically powered devices. The company offers a range of brick-format DC-DC converters, complementary components for AC line rectification and filtering, and input/output voltage products. Vicor serves customers in the United States, Europe, Asia Pacific, and internationally, and is known for its high-performance power management solutions.

ticker_wolf.name: Wolfspeed, Inc.
ticker_wolf.blurb: Wolfspeed designs and manufactures silicon carbide (SiC) power devices and substrates, positioning itself as the only vertically integrated producer at 200mm SiC wafer scale. Carved out of Cree in 2021, the company bet heavily on the EV and industrial power transition, sinking billions into the John Palmour Manufacturing Center in North Carolina and the Mohawk Valley Fab in New York. The ambition was sound; the balance sheet was not. After accumulating roughly $4.6 billion in debt and missing the expected CHIPS Act funding of $750 million, Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on June 30, 2025. It emerged ninety-one days later in a prepackaged restructuring that eliminated ~70% of its debt, extended maturities to 2030, and cut annual cash interest expense by roughly 60%. Existing shareholders received only 3–5% of the reorganised equity; the bulk went to convertible noteholders (56.3%) and strategic investor Renesas (38.7%), who received new common stock plus warrants.
ticker_wolf.recent: Post-emergence, the reorganised Wolfspeed trades on NYSE under WOLF. The company's enterprise value at emergence was estimated at $2.35–2.85 billion (midpoint $2.6B), implying equity of $850M–$1.35B. As of May 2026 shares trade near $38. A December 2025 IRS settlement worth roughly $698 million provided unexpected cash relief. Chinese SiC substrate producers SICC (688234.SS) and TanKeBlue have gained market share during Wolfspeed's restructuring, while Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, and Rohm continue to invest in competing SiC capacity.

poster_citrini.blurb: Independent thematic-equity research firm founded in 2023 by James van Geelen, a self-taught investor who began his career in alternative healthcare before turning to public markets in 2018. Citrini publishes via paid Substack, runs a portfolio of long/short thematic baskets called the Citrindex, and has built a following on X for early calls on AI 'picks and shovels,' GLP-1 obesity drugs, and idiosyncratic trades such as a public short of Silicon Valley Bank in late 2022, months before its collapse. The firm now reports roughly ten employees and covers themes spanning AI, robotics, defence, healthcare and government policy.
poster_citrini.credibility_note: Track-record claims are largely self-reported through paywalled subscriber notes; the firm's '+131% since inception' and '+100% one-year' figures for its core portfolio cannot be audited externally. That said, several specific calls have been corroborated in the public press: the early 2023 AI hardware basket, the SVB short, and a February 2026 note on AI capex sustainability that was credited by Bloomberg with helping trigger an equity-market sell-off. Van Geelen, born around 1992, holds bachelor's degrees in biology and psychology from UCLA and is not a CFA charterholder; positions described in Citrini notes are the firm's own, and readers should assume the firm transacts in the names it covers.
